architecture.caption: The browser never receives the Gemini server key. Firebase identifies the user; MongoDB owns app records. Browser working history is a separate persistence path.

auth.caption: After the owned profile read, these are three different outcomes. A 500, HTML response or timeout is never evidence that a profile is absent.

nutrition.caption: The server is the correctness boundary even if client target ensure and menu generation start concurrently. A completed invalid response can receive one correction; transport failures cannot.

nodes: weekly save is not a transaction
models.caption: These are logical relationships using the Firebase UID string, not automatic ObjectId foreign keys. ChatHistory also has a schema/read endpoint, but message sends do not persist it.

reuse.caption: Custom targets do not need target estimation. In auto mode, valid targets are reused unless inputs change, an explicit review is requested, or the configured weight threshold is reached.

chat.caption: The edge from greeting to classification means "if it is not a pure greeting". A scope gate limits answer scope, but still costs a classifier request and is not a rate limiter.

async.caption: Illustrates completion order, not measured latency. Cancellation saves work when supported; the revision check prevents stale results from updating the current account.

weight.caption: Sparse measurements remain sparse. Activity streaks use logged meals/movement, not whether a person shared weight.

deploy.caption: This is the configured deployment design, not an availability or production-load claim. Set VITE_API_URL to the Render API base including /api.

pages.title: How to use this guide
pages.goal: Build understanding you can demonstrate without reading a script.

blocks.title: What this is
blocks.body: A source-based study guide for AI Guruji at commit 16c4932, audited on 8 November 2026. It explains the current Gemini implementation, reusable targets and personalized schedules. Earlier Groq, fixed-four-meal and light-theme descriptions in historical notes are superseded.

blocks.title: Three passes
rows: Read architecture, authentication and storage pages. Draw the system from memory.
Name every network boundary and data owner.
Follow one meal request, one weigh-in and one chat from button to response.
Open the source at the references and explain each step.
Solve the coding exercises in a practice branch; run the relevant tests.
Make a small change, explain failure cases, and test it.

blocks.title: Study rule
blocks.body: Read an answer once, close it, explain it aloud in your own words, then reopen the exact source. Memorize invariants and flows before memorizing filenames. If you cannot explain a line, turn it into a question.

blocks.title: Verification boundary
blocks.body: This audit ran 19 client tests, 54 backend tests and a production client build successfully under Node 24.13.0. Provider tests mock HTTP. No paid model requests, real-account changes, deployed load tests or live end-to-end sign-in were performed for these notes.

pages.title: A seven-day preparation plan
pages.goal: Use the project as a practical full-stack course.

blocks.title: Daily route: about 90-120 minutes
rows: Draw five components and explain browser vs server data.
React state, auth, routing and startup
Trace loading -> user/profile -> dashboard or onboarding.
Calculate a macro example; reject a shortfall and a duplicate slot.
Trace a meal rebuild while preserving consumed calories.
Explain measured/reused/skipped; count chat model calls.
Diagnose 401, 429, 503, a stale menu and a lost browser cache.
Give a two-minute demo, answer follow-ups, solve two exercises.

blocks.title: Use a four-point mastery scale
items: 0: I recognize the term but cannot explain it.
1: I can describe the idea with notes.
2: I can trace it in this code without notes.
3: I can change it safely and write a test that would catch a regression.

blocks.title: When you are ready to call this your main project
blocks.body: Aim for level 3 in authentication ownership, nutrition validation, browser/server persistence and the chatbot pipeline. Do not claim expertise in every library simply because it appears in package.json.

pages.title: Your project story and AI-assisted ownership
pages.goal: Present the work honestly, with specific evidence.

blocks.title: A 45-second project explanation
blocks.body: "AI Guruji is a personal fitness companion focused on Indian food preferences and practical routines. Users save their goals, generate daily meal plans and weekly workouts, log food and movement, track optional weigh-ins, and ask short follow-up questions about their plans. React handles the experience, Express handles authenticated orchestration, Firebase identifies users, MongoDB stores profiles and key records, and Gemini generates structured plans and coach replies. A major engineering challenge is validating AI output and preserving the user's recorded history when plans change."

blocks.title: If asked how much AI wrote
blocks.body: "A substantial part of the implementation was AI-assisted. I am not claiming I typed every line manually. My responsibility is to understand the design, verify behavior and maintain it. I can walk through the authentication boundary, the target-validation pipeline, the storage tradeoffs and a change with tests." Use the last sentence only after you can actually demonstrate it.

blocks.title: Evidence to bring
items: Trace one request in the source instead of naming technologies only.
Explain one limitation before the interviewer discovers it.
Show a regression test and why it matters.
Distinguish a feature you requested/reviewed from a line of code you personally authored.

blocks.title: CV wording you can adapt
blocks.body: "Developed an AI-assisted personal fitness application using React, Express, MongoDB, Firebase Authentication and Gemini, with validated nutrition planning, optional weight tracking and scoped trainer follow-ups." Add test counts only with a date/snapshot. Do not invent usage, accuracy, latency, uptime or weight-loss metrics.

pages.title: The whole system in one picture
pages.goal: Explain the system before explaining individual components.

blocks.title: Why these responsibilities are separated
blocks.body: The browser renders screens and maintains a working journal. Express is the place to verify tokens, choose the owned database record, call the model and validate results before saving. Firebase is the identity service; it is not the fitness database. The model is an external dependency, not a database or an authorization engine.

blocks.title: Why a monolith is reasonable here
blocks.body: There are two independent npm packages, not separate microservices for every feature. This keeps deployment and debugging manageable for a personal project. Services and pure contracts separate domain logic without adding network hops.

blocks.title: Say it precisely
blocks.body: This is an API-backed React single-page application with server-side AI orchestration. It is not a trained-from-scratch model, a vector-search/RAG system, or an autonomous tool-using agent.

pages.title: Your source-code navigation map
pages.goal: Know where to look instead of scanning the whole repository.

blocks.title: Follow the responsibility
rows: React root, auth provider, route decisions
Owned weight journal and save state

blocks.title: Read in this order for an unfamiliar feature
items: UI event -> backendService helper -> Express route -> verifyToken -> controller -> domain service/model -> response -> state/cache update.
Read docs/ARCHITECTURE.md as an index. Read current source before answering; historical migration notes may describe obsolete behavior.
The file name deepseekService.js is historical. The actual provider adapter imports Gemini.

pages.title: Authentication: prove who owns a request
pages.goal: Separate identity, authorization and profile existence.

blocks.title: Explain the boundary
blocks.body: The Firebase client signs the person in. Axios obtains an ID token and puts it in Authorization: Bearer. The Admin SDK verifies it on the server, and controllers use req.user.uid for ownership. A body field named uid or userId is not proof of identity. The frontend route guard improves navigation; it does not protect the API by itself.

blocks.title: Important security-review exception
blocks.body: The intended rule is verified ownership. The workout save currently spreads generated day fields after ownership/date fields; that weaker boundary needs an explicit allowlist and server-owned fields assigned last. Do not claim every write is immune to ownership override.

pages.title: Routes, startup and the cold-start loader
pages.goal: A slow backend is a different state from a new user.

blocks.title: Observed state -> UI decision
rows: Show StartupScreen; never hide all provider children.
Show public landing/auth; start one bounded anonymous warm-up.
Open dashboard; existing profile has view mode and a separate editor.
Retry safe reads, then show connection error with Retry.
Accessible while session/profile loading or errors continue.

blocks.title: Know the actual limits
blocks.body: Profile/readiness reads have a 120-second total window, 15-second attempt limits and 2.5-second gaps. Initial Firebase restoration has a separate 20-second timeout. AbortController and revision checks stop an old session from updating a new one. This is not a permanent keep-alive and does not prevent the host from sleeping.

blocks.title: Why reads and writes differ
blocks.body: A safe profile/readiness GET can be attempted again. Replaying a plan-generation POST could incur model cost and save extra snapshots. The startup helper does not globally retry writes, swaps or chat.

blocks.title: Health is deliberately limited
blocks.body: /api/health is public, no-store JSON: 200 ready or 503 starting. It checks MongoDB connection and Firebase Admin initialization, not Gemini quota, model access or every database operation.

pages.title: The data model and its guarantees
pages.goal: Explain why indexes and document structure matter.

blocks.title: Index distinction
rows: Unique application profile per Firebase UID.
Unique date entry per user; changing a check-in replaces that date.
Query index only, not uniqueness. Multiple snapshots can exist.
Model/read endpoint exists; sendMessage does not write conversation history.

blocks.title: Embedding versus references
blocks.body: Meals and exercises are embedded in plan documents because they belong to a generated snapshot and are commonly read together. User linkage is a string UID. Mongoose provides schemas and queries, but an ordinary index does not create referential integrity or make a multi-document write transactional.

pages.title: Persistence: the most important tradeoff
pages.goal: Know what survives a different browser or cleared storage.

blocks.title: Current ownership map
rows: DB history exists; dashboard does not hydrate it.
Working activity does not currently sync.

blocks.title: Answer the two-device question honestly
blocks.body: A second device can recover the profile and weight journal, but it cannot reconstruct local completion, manual logs, swaps or the browser conversation. Clearing local cache can trigger generation again even though a plan snapshot is stored in MongoDB. Synchronizing this requires owned journal endpoints plus explicit merge/version semantics; it is not solved by merely adding a history GET.

blocks.title: Namespacing is not authorization
blocks.body: A UID in a localStorage key prevents accidental mixing in normal app reads. It does not encrypt the data, protect it from XSS, or remove prior account data on logout.

pages.title: React state: the concepts you must explain
pages.goal: Connect hooks and immutability to a real bug class.

blocks.title: State versus derived values
blocks.body: Dashboard owns working day state and passes data/callbacks to cards. useState triggers a render; useRef holds mutable bookkeeping without causing one; useEffect synchronizes external work and returns cleanup; useCallback stabilizes a function for specified dependencies. Derived values such as burnedToday should come from current inputs rather than a second unsynchronized copy.

blocks.title: Why the extended array matters
blocks.body: A state setter schedules a future render; it does not mutate the current closure. addManualWorkout computes burn from updatedWorkouts immediately, instead of calling a helper that still sees the old array. Completion IDs, burn and net energy are saved together. For updates based only on previous state, a functional setter such as setItems(old => [...old, item]) avoids capturing an outdated array.

blocks.title: Likely follow-ups
items: Why are arrays copied instead of mutated? New references make updates predictable and avoid hidden shared mutation.
Why does StrictMode expose duplicate effects? Development replay reveals missing cleanup and duplicate side effects; it is not a reason to remove StrictMode.
Why a custom hook? useProgress and useNutritionProfile isolate async state/lifecycle logic from rendering. They are not globally shared state just because they are hooks.

pages.title: Nutrition: understand the full pipeline
pages.goal: Separate target estimation, menu construction and validation.

blocks.title: Two different model jobs
blocks.body: Auto target estimation decides reusable daily numeric targets from the saved goal/body/activity inputs and latest actual weight. Menu generation constructs meals for the saved schedule using those fixed targets. A new day normally needs a new menu, not a fresh target estimate. Custom macros skip target estimation entirely.

blocks.title: The server remains authoritative
blocks.body: The client can ensure target state through useNutritionProfile while a generation request is also starting. Both paths reach server-side target resolution. Client readiness, disabled buttons and displayed totals are useful UX, but only server validation decides whether a generated plan is eligible for saving.

blocks.title: What makes this more than a prompt wrapper
blocks.body: The application adds owned profile lookup, target persistence, schedule identity, arithmetic checks, bounded correction, stale-profile checks, worker-local coalescing, local journaling and explicit rebuild behavior around the model call.

pages.title: When should nutrition targets change?
pages.goal: Defend reuse and refresh rules with numbers.

blocks.title: Worked example: cumulative weight change
blocks.body: Suppose the saved target basis is 80 kg and the threshold is 5%. A measurement of 76.1 kg differs by 3.9/80 = 4.875%, so the current targets can remain. At 76.0 kg the absolute difference is 5%, so auto targets need review on the next resolve. Compare with the saved basis, not only yesterday: small cumulative changes can eventually cross the threshold. A successful refresh resets the basis.

blocks.title: Signatures have different jobs
blocks.body: targetInputKey includes age, gender, height, goal, activity, macro mode and custom grams. Weight is handled separately. nutritionProfileKey also includes the schedule and food/preferences/allergies/region/budget/notes. Name/email changes do not invalidate nutrition. The signature is JSON serialization for comparison, not a cryptographic signature or an authorization mechanism.

blocks.title: Custom targets and concurrency
blocks.body: Custom grams remain authoritative even after a large weight change. Conditional User writes prevent selected stale profile updates, but the filters are not a full transaction or a guarantee against every concurrent new weigh-in race.

pages.title: Meal schedules: three identities, three jobs
pages.goal: Never use meal type as a unique identity.

blocks.title: Do not confuse these fields
rows: Stable place in the saved schedule.
Specific meal instance used by completion tracking.
User-facing meaning and optional schedule time.

blocks.title: Current contract
blocks.body: A saved schedule contains 2-6 slots. Slot IDs must be distinct lowercase alphanumeric/hyphen strings; labels must be nonempty and at most 50 characters; optional time is validated as HH:MM. A generated menu must contain exactly one meal per slot and must preserve schedule order. Two snacks remain independent because their slot IDs differ.

blocks.title: Backward compatibility
blocks.body: Old plans without a saved schedule use the default four-slot mapping. Presentation keeps extra old meals readable. Historical cards use their own saved schedule and targets, not the current profile preferences. Rebuilding the current menu is explicit.

blocks.title: Why mirror the contract?
blocks.body: Client and backend each deploy from their own package root. Pure contract copies keep each package self-contained; a behavioral parity test detects drift. A future shared versioned package is an option, not the current architecture.

pages.title: Validation: a worked nutrition example
pages.goal: Explain what validation proves and what it cannot prove.

blocks.title: Example fixed targets, for software arithmetic only
Energy consistency
blocks.body: The example macro energy is 150*4 + 225*4 + 56*9 = 2,004 kcal, consistent with a 2,000 kcal target. A meal containing 40 g protein, 50 g carbs and 15 g fat implies 495 kcal. If it declares 500 kcal, the difference is 1% of the declared calories, within the meal-level 15% check. These are illustrative arithmetic values, not a recommended diet.

blocks.title: A valid shape can still be wrong
blocks.body: JSON schema checks structure/types. The domain validator additionally checks scheduled slot completeness, distinctness, recipes, finite nutrition values, daily totals and per-meal macro energy. A plan with 149 g protein fails a 150 g minimum even if its calories are perfect. totalCalories is derived from meals rather than accepted independently.

blocks.title: Do not overclaim nutritional accuracy
blocks.body: The checks establish internal consistency and target bounds, not truthful ingredient nutrition, allergen exclusion or clinical suitability. The app has no verified food-composition database or deterministic allergen engine.

pages.title: Generate a daily menu: trace the code
pages.goal: Follow the owned request all the way to the working cache.

blocks.title: Button to response
items: Dashboard calls generateDietPlan(), which POSTs /api/diet/generate without trusting a client-supplied profile.
verifyToken sets req.user. createDietPlan resolves that UID's profile/targets and forms a pending-plan key from UID, UTC day, profile signature and fixed targets.
Gemini receives profile data, the fixed targets and the exact saved meal slots. Completed text is parsed and domain-validated.
Before saving, the controller reads the current profile and rejects a mismatching menu signature/target set.
DietPlan.create saves a snapshot. Dashboard caches a dated working copy, initializes tracking if missing and refreshes target profile state.

blocks.title: What coalescing means
blocks.body: Simultaneous matching requests in one Node worker await the same Promise. This reduces duplicate estimation/menu calls during concurrent requests and development effect replay. The entry is removed in finally. It is not permanent caching, a distributed lock, global idempotency, or a unique account/day database constraint.

blocks.title: Failure behavior
blocks.body: A failed target estimate/menu leaves prior saved targets or the working menu intact. Nutrition provider rate errors propagate as 429; availability/configuration errors as 503. A stale-profile conflict is 409. Do not label all failures as missing profile.

pages.title: Swaps and rebuilds must preserve history
pages.goal: Do not erase what the user already consumed.

blocks.title: One-meal swap
blocks.body: The browser sends the current meal plus the working plan. The server reads the owned profile, checks current signature/targets when a plan is supplied, and validates the replacement in the whole-day context. A snack replacement must retain that exact slot ID; another snack is left alone. A new meal instance ID allows distinct completion tracking. The browser recalculates plan calories and tracking targets. The swap does not update the saved MongoDB snapshot.

blocks.title: Worked rebuild example
blocks.body: A user logged breakfast (460 kcal) and lunch (610 kcal), so consumed energy is 1,070 kcal. They now change five scheduled meals to three and explicitly rebuild. retainLoggedMeals moves completed old planned meals into the manual journal using the original IDs, deduplicating against existing manual entries. Consumed energy, completed IDs and movement history remain; the new target comes from the new menu. Unlogged old meals are not fabricated as eaten.

blocks.title: What to test
blocks.body: Repeated snack slots, a swap that drops protein below the daily target, stale profile signatures, a rebuilt day with old completed food, duplicate retained IDs and failure leaving the original menu untouched.

pages.title: Training: explain the weaker path too
pages.goal: A truthful project explanation includes uneven maturity.

blocks.title: Happy path
blocks.body: The client requests a week starting on the selected date. The prompt asks for seven chronological days, meaningful session focus and appropriate recovery days. The service parses weekPlan, assigns exercise IDs and uses the focus or dayName. The controller saves each returned day with Promise.all; the client assigns consecutive dates by array position and caches each day.

blocks.title: Current limitations you should be ready to discuss
items: The controller stamps the same UTC today date on each entry unless a spread day overrides it. The browser corrects display dates locally; database history dates still need a real fix.
Promise.all is concurrent, not a transaction. A partial save can survive if another write fails.
Workout structure/date ordering has weaker domain validation than nutrition. Generated day fields are spread after userId/date, so assign server-owned fields last and allowlist output.
Provider failure returns a static beginner week with no explicit fallback marker. This must not be presented as a successful personalized generation.

blocks.title: Recovery versus missing data
blocks.body: An actual saved session with an empty exercises array can represent recovery. A missing saved plan means unknown/no data, not automatically a recovery day or a missed workout.

pages.title: Progress: measured, reused and skipped
pages.goal: Keep an honest record of what is known.

blocks.title: Why the write is robust
blocks.body: The ownership filter is built from req.user.uid plus the validated date. A compound unique index enforces one check-in per account/date; upsert inserts or replaces it. On duplicate-key error 11000 from an insertion race, the controller repeats the update without upsert. A reused entry is resolved from the latest earlier actual measurement on the server, ignoring any browser-supplied weight/source.

blocks.title: Future personalization
blocks.body: withLatestWeight overlays the latest measured weight in transient AI context and leaves the profile baseline intact. It excludes future, reused and skipped entries. A new measurement can inform target review; it does not automatically replace a menu the user already logged.

pages.title: Numbers, charts and calendar days
pages.goal: Explain formulas without confusing them with health outcomes.

blocks.title: Current calculation
rows: Sum of logged meal energy. Example: 460+610 = 1,070 kcal.
Estimated energy for completed exercises/manual movement.
Target - consumed. 1,900 - 1,070 = 830; does not subtract burn.
Latest actual measurement - first actual in selected range.
Consecutive days with a meal/exercise log; an empty today can be skipped.

blocks.title: Manual movement is an estimate
blocks.body: The modal uses round(minutes * intensityRate * weight/70), with rates 3.5, 7 and 11. Missing/invalid weight falls back to 70 kg. This is an app estimate, not wearable-measured expenditure or a clinical energy-balance engine. Unlogged days are unknown, not proof of non-adherence.

blocks.title: The UTC trap
blocks.body: dayKey uses toISOString().slice(0,10). At 01:00 on 8 November in India, UTC is still 7 November. Some calendar helpers use UTC-safe day arithmetic while older dashboard loops use local setDate then ISO. A fix must cover cache keys, server dates, charts, history, migration and midnight rollover together; changing one formatter does not fix the data model.

blocks.title: Trend honesty
blocks.body: weightSummary includes only actual measured points. Two actual observations are needed for a change. Reused values do not create extra points, and scale-weight change is not a body-fat measurement.

pages.title: The chatbot is a trainer follow-up channel
pages.goal: Explain the branches and their cost.

blocks.title: Examples you should predict
rows: Deterministic short greeting; no provider request.
Can I replace paneer in lunch?
In scope; classify, then contextual answer.
Plan request; direct user to plan screens.
Write Python for my calorie tracker
Off topic, even though calories are fitness-related.

blocks.title: Why scope excludes old assistant replies
blocks.body: The classifier gets the latest message and up to four recent user messages truncated to 500 characters each. Saved profile data and assistant messages are excluded so an old fitness goal or strict response does not transform an unrelated request into a fitness task. Relevant answering then uses profile, recent conversation and summarized plan context.

pages.title: Prompts, context and safe presentation
pages.goal: Distinguish useful controls from guarantees.

blocks.title: What is supplied to the answer model
blocks.body: The coach policy asks for short practical help about meals, exercise and recovery. Saved profile context excludes UID/email and includes relevant preferences and saved targets. The answer history is normalized to user/assistant roles and capped at 12 messages. Browser working-plan context is projected into bounded meal/exercise fields rather than passed through wholesale.

blocks.title: A browser plan is advisory
blocks.body: The snapshot can include local swaps and incomplete data. summarizePlanContext keeps useful fields, trims text and bounds lists, and labels the data as a browser snapshot. It is not an authenticated server record and must not be interpreted as instructions. Missing meals stay unknown; an empty actual workout can mean recovery.

blocks.title: Why users do not see raw ** markers
blocks.body: ChatMessage converts a small Markdown subset into React elements: emphasis, code, headings, lists and paragraphs. It never evaluates raw HTML. React escapes ordinary strings, so text such as an img/onerror tag remains text. This is not a full Markdown/link/table renderer and not a claim that all possible XSS sources in the app have been audited.

blocks.title: Scope is not credit-abuse prevention by itself
blocks.body: The classifier is model-based, may misclassify, and still costs a request. The project has no per-account rate limiter or hard budget system. A serious abuse-control layer needs those independent server-side controls.

pages.title: Gemini integration: know the exact boundary
pages.goal: Explain configuration and failure behavior without exposing keys.

blocks.title: Current implementation
rows: geminiClient.js lazily creates GoogleGenAI; prompts stay in deepseekService.js.
GEMINI_MODEL, default gemini-3.6-flash; provider availability is not verified here.
GEMINI_API_KEY, then GOOGLE_API_KEY; never a VITE_ client secret.
Native user_input/model_output steps; store:false; no streaming or tools.
Nonempty text only when response.status is completed.
429 -> AI_RATE_LIMIT; credential/model access -> AI_CONFIGURATION; other failures -> AI_UNAVAILABLE.

blocks.title: Structured output is the first layer
blocks.body: JSON tasks request an application/json schema; nutrition/scope have explicit requirements, while workout uses a more generic object shape. Parsed output still needs domain validation. store:false is a request setting, not a blanket guarantee about a provider's total data-handling policy.

blocks.title: One correction is not an automatic network replay
blocks.body: Nutrition may make one additional call after a completed response fails JSON/domain validation. It includes the prior output and validation error while keeping targets fixed. If no completed response was received, the failure propagates immediately. Menu/target/swap corrections are bounded per stage, not free or unlimited.

pages.title: Asynchronous code and concurrency
pages.goal: Tell cancellation, stale suppression and coalescing apart.

blocks.title: Three mechanisms
rows: Does not undo a write already committed.
Ignore results for old sessions or obsolete requests.
Do not serialize every server operation.
Share simultaneous matching work in one worker.
Not a distributed lock, permanent cache or idempotency key.
Reject certain changed profile states before saving.
Not a full transaction across all collections.

blocks.title: Explain await and Promise.all
blocks.body: await suspends the async function, not the entire Node process. Promise.all waits for a group and rejects when one rejects; other operations may still run. That is why a weekly save can be partially persisted. Always distinguish an in-memory concurrency optimization from a durable database guarantee.

pages.title: Deployment and configuration
pages.goal: Trace a production request without revealing credentials.

blocks.title: What to configure
items: Use Node 24 from .nvmrc and the package engine declarations. Each package has its own tracked lockfile; npm ci installs the locked tree.
Build client with npm run build. Vercel serves its static output and rewrites SPA paths to index.html. These rewrites do not automatically proxy the API to Render.
Set VITE_API_URL to the backend base including /api. VITE_ values are included in the browser bundle; keep model keys and Firebase Admin private keys on the backend.
Set the backend MongoDB, Firebase Admin, Gemini and frontend-origin environment values. Do not paste credential values into a README, browser console, CV or screenshot.
Render config uses backend as rootDir, npm ci, npm start and /api/health as healthCheckPath. A readiness failure is different from model quota/access failure.

blocks.title: CORS is not authentication
blocks.body: CORS governs browser cross-origin access. A script outside a browser is not stopped by CORS. Every protected route still needs a verified bearer token and owned queries; avoid describing FRONTEND_URL as the security boundary.

pages.title: Security review: controls and gaps
pages.goal: Make qualified claims you can defend in source.

blocks.title: Threat model
rows: Verified token UID; owned queries in profile/progress/nutrition paths.
Allowlist workout output and assign server-owned fields last.
Gemini/Admin credentials stay on server; public web config is separate.
Redact raw model/health-context logs and maintain secret hygiene.
Role/policy separation; bounded projected plan data; scope gate.
Model-based controls are not guaranteed jailbreak prevention.
Greeting bypass, scope gate, token limits, target reuse, worker coalescing.
Per-account rate limits, quotas, request budgets and abuse monitoring.
Explicit cleanup/export policy; XSS defenses and storage recovery.
Comprehensive demographic validation; verified email policy.

blocks.title: Own the workout boundary issue
blocks.body: Workout day data is spread after userId/date and has weaker validation. The intended identity invariant should be enforced after allowlisting model fields, not merely requested in a prompt. In an interview, explain how you would test an output containing a forged userId/date and prove it cannot change persistence ownership.

blocks.title: Do not say production-secure
blocks.body: Tests and a token middleware are useful evidence, not a complete security audit. Discuss controls, gaps, priorities and verification methods separately.

pages.title: Limitations and the next sensible iteration
pages.goal: A mature answer does not hide unfinished boundaries.

blocks.title: Prioritized follow-up work
rows: Workout output ownership/date safety and weak validation.
Allowlisted normalized output; verified ownership last; actual day sequence validation + tests.
Activity/chat working history stays in the browser.
Owned journal APIs, server hydration, versioned merge and offline conflict rules.
No durable generation idempotency across workers.
Request keys, uniqueness/version policy and a distributed/durable claim of work.
Typed status/fallback markers and honest recovery UI.
UTC/local day mismatch and no midnight rollover.
Define user timezone and migrate cache/history consistently.
No rate limits, full privacy controls or CI.
Add budget/rate policy, export/delete semantics and automated checks.

blocks.title: What is intentionally out of scope now
blocks.body: No body-image analysis, vector retrieval, wearable integration, model training, streaming answers or automatic plan execution by chat is implemented. Nutrition estimates are internally checked but not clinically verified. A weight chart alone cannot prove fat loss or causal effectiveness.

blocks.title: How to frame a weakness
blocks.body: "The current version does X. That creates limitation Y. I would change Z and verify it with these tests." Avoid saying a future feature already exists, or promising that a generated plan is medically accurate.

pages.title: Testing: explain what the evidence means
pages.goal: Tests should protect behavior, not imitate implementation.

blocks.title: Fresh verification on 8 November 2026
rows: Formatting safety, retained logs, schedule/status logic, trends, dates, startup cancellation.
Token ownership, progress rules, target reuse/CAS, schedule parity, validation and mocked SDK transport.
The frontend compiles into production assets.
No claim of real-model reliability, real-account E2E success, load capacity or availability.

blocks.title: A strong example
blocks.body: The protein-shortfall tests ensure an 87 g day cannot satisfy a fixed 130 g target, even if model text claims it is sufficient. The provider 429 test mocks HTTP and asserts one request, preventing accidental paid retries. The reused/skipped trend test ensures a chart does not fabricate measurements.

blocks.title: What still needs coverage
blocks.body: Add an actual authenticated browser/API happy path, deployed CORS/rewrites/health checks, model-output ownership/date hardening, cross-worker idempotency, and a reproducible evaluation set for chatbot scope. Existing Node tests are not an end-to-end or load-test suite.

blocks.title: Commands to reproduce
blocks.body: From the repo use Node 24. Run npm test separately in client/ and backend/, then npm run build in client/. Do not run from the parent folder: there is no root npm workspace. Avoid live paid provider requests just to prove a unit test passes.

pages.title: Debugging drill: blank page or wrong onboarding
pages.goal: Walk through evidence before changing keys or prompts.

blocks.title: Symptom -> investigation
rows: HTML fallback, AuthProvider children, route loading/error guards.
Rendering must not depend on the slow profile result.

blocks.title: Use a diagnostic sequence
blocks.body: Confirm the actual browser request URL, HTTP status and response type. Confirm server route and health. Check authentication separately from AI access. Then inspect saved profile/targets and the model error category. Never log complete bearer tokens, private keys or whole health profiles while debugging.

blocks.q: Would you automatically retry a failed generation POST?
blocks.a: Not with the startup read helper. A failed response does not prove the model was never charged or the database never saved. First define idempotency and recovery behavior; then decide which failures are safe to replay.

pages.title: Debugging drill: wrong meals, totals or dates
pages.goal: Trace the source of truth for each symptom.

blocks.title: Symptom -> source -> verification
rows: Changing model/key appears to do nothing
Inspect the correct UID/day key; cached plans are not auto-regenerated.
Two snack slots collapse into one
Trace normalization and swap selection; test distinct IDs.
Compare input key and measured weight with saved basis.
Offer explicit rebuild; retain consumed food and historical snapshots.
Only measured entries should become points; skipped is null, not zero.
Validate and assign actual date per index before owned persistence.

blocks.q: Why can a total be internally consistent yet still inaccurate?
blocks.a: The model may estimate an ingredient's nutrition incorrectly while keeping 4/4/9 energy and daily totals consistent. Arithmetic checks do not verify a food database or allergen safety.

blocks.q: Why does my plan differ after switching browsers?
blocks.a: The dashboard does not hydrate the server history into its working cache. The profile and weight journal can be recovered, but local activities/swaps/chat cannot currently be reconstructed.

rows: Mixed measured/reused/skipped input returns only actual points and correct first/last change.
A total of 149 g fails a 150 g target, even when calories fit.

blocks.title: Hints to check after trying
blocks.body: Filter by status before sorting weights. Compare protein with the target before accepting any tolerance. Use slotId for a place in the schedule and id for an instance. Use a Set for deduplication, not meal names. Preserve completion/consumption history when target/schedule changes.

blocks.title: Your proof of completion
blocks.body: Write a failing test before the fix, then make it pass. Explain why the old behavior fails, which invariant your change protects, and which unrelated behavior stays intact. Do the exercises in a practice branch; they are not changes implemented by this document.

pages.title: Coding practice: boundary and concurrency tasks
pages.goal: Move from explaining code to defending a change.

blocks.title: More demanding exercises
rows: A generated forged userId/date cannot override verified ownership; exactly seven valid ordered dates; recovery day shape explicit.
Exact missing-profile 404 permits onboarding; HTML 404, 401, 503 and timeout cannot be silently treated as absence.
Start A, start B, resolve B then A; only B updates the current screen. Abort/unmount prevents later updates.
Design {status, source, data, error} for workout/chat failures and explain a backward-compatible rollout.
Specify ownership, event IDs, versioning, conflict resolution and migration before writing hydration code.

blocks.title: Suggested approach for task 6
blocks.body: Parse provider output into a fresh allowlisted object. Validate chronological dates using one consistent day contract. Assign userId from req.user.uid and the date from server logic after normalization. Add a test where the provider includes unexpected ownership/date fields. Then decide whether weekly persistence needs a transaction or a job status.

blocks.title: Do not bypass the interview exercise
blocks.body: If you get stuck, write down the exact unknown: array transformation, async order, database filter, HTTP semantics or React lifecycle. Study that concept, then retry from a blank file. Copying a polished answer does not demonstrate maintainability.

pages.title: React and browser fundamentals
pages.goal: Close each answer and explain it in your own words.

blocks.q: What happens after a user logs in?
blocks.a: Firebase returns identity; AuthProvider loads the owned profile through Axios, shows startup state, then route guards choose dashboard or genuine onboarding. A request failure stays a connection error.
blocks.probe: Trace a returning user and a new user separately.

blocks.q: Why use Context here?
blocks.a: The Firebase user, MongoDB profile and session actions are needed by several screens. Context exposes that shared state without passing it through every intermediate component. It is not the persistence layer.
blocks.probe: What belongs in local component state instead?

blocks.q: Why is useRef useful for a revision?
blocks.a: It survives renders without causing one. Comparing a request's captured revision to the current ref lets the hook ignore late results from an obsolete operation.
blocks.probe: Why is abort alone insufficient?

blocks.q: Why not mutate the meals array?
blocks.a: A copied array makes state changes explicit and avoids mutating an object shared by the prior render. Replacement also lets React observe a new reference.
blocks.probe: When is a functional state setter preferable?

blocks.q: What does useEffect cleanup do?
blocks.a: It unsubscribes Firebase listeners, aborts pending reads or invalidates a request revision when the component/effect is replaced. Cleanup prevents stale work from updating the wrong session.
blocks.probe: Explain StrictMode development replay.

blocks.q: Why stable IDs rather than array indexes?
blocks.a: The UI needs to track the same semantic item across ordering or replacement. A schedule slot ID and a generated completion ID solve different identity problems; a render index cannot replace either.
blocks.probe: What changes on a meal swap?

blocks.q: Why a route guard if the server verifies tokens?
blocks.a: The guard directs users to sign-in/onboarding and shows loading/errors. The server remains the authorization boundary for actual data access. Both are needed for different reasons.
blocks.probe: Can a user bypass a frontend guard?

blocks.q: Is localStorage a secure database?
blocks.a: It is synchronous, origin-scoped browser storage. It is convenient for this working journal but is readable by JavaScript, device-local and currently lacks quota/recovery/cleanup handling.
blocks.probe: What would happen after logout on a shared computer?

pages.title: HTTP, backend and databases
pages.goal: Close each answer and explain it in your own words.

blocks.q: Why Express routes, controllers and services?
blocks.a: Routes connect URLs to verified handlers; controllers translate HTTP and ownership into operations; services hold domain/provider logic; models define persistence. This makes policy and arithmetic testable without a live UI.
blocks.probe: Where should a macro validation rule live?

blocks.q: Authentication versus authorization?
blocks.a: Authentication proves the token identity. Authorization ensures an operation is scoped to that verified UID and allowed resource. A valid token does not authorize another account's records.
blocks.probe: Show the owned progress filter.

blocks.q: What is an upsert?
blocks.a: It updates a matching document or inserts if none matches. Weight writes use verified UID plus date, together with a unique compound index, so the journal has one dated entry per account.
blocks.probe: Why handle duplicate-key error 11000?

blocks.q: Why not a unique index on all plan dates?
blocks.a: Plans currently store generated snapshots, and explicit sequential rebuilds may produce more than one. Changing uniqueness requires defining versions, current-plan selection and migration, not simply adding a constraint.
blocks.probe: How would idempotency differ from snapshot versioning?

blocks.q: Does Promise.all make writes atomic?
blocks.a: No. It coordinates concurrent promises; one rejection does not roll back writes that already succeeded. Weekly persistence needs an explicit transaction or an explicit partial/job model if atomicity is required.
blocks.probe: What happens if day four fails?

blocks.q: What does HTTP 409 mean here?
blocks.a: A conflict: preferences/targets changed while an operation was in progress, so its result should not be saved as current. The user can retry using the new state.
blocks.probe: Why not return a successful stale menu?

blocks.q: Why is CORS not enough?
blocks.a: It constrains browser cross-origin behavior, not arbitrary HTTP clients. The API still needs token verification, owned queries, input validation and resource controls.
blocks.probe: Can curl ignore the browser's CORS policy?

blocks.q: What belongs in a health endpoint?
blocks.a: A minimal non-sensitive readiness result with no-store cache policy. This implementation checks MongoDB and Admin initialization but deliberately does not spend a model call or expose profile/secret details.
blocks.probe: Readiness versus liveness?

pages.title: Nutrition, identity and validation
pages.goal: Close each answer and explain it in your own words.

blocks.q: Why resolve targets before meals?
blocks.a: It gives generation a stable numeric contract and lets unchanged goals reuse targets. The model cannot excuse a protein shortfall by redefining the target after seeing the menu.
blocks.probe: What changes in custom mode?

blocks.q: Why a separate signature for targets and menus?
blocks.a: Body/goal/activity changes can affect target estimates; schedule/food preferences affect meal composition. Separating them avoids unnecessary target estimation while still identifying outdated menus.
blocks.probe: Why are name and email excluded?

blocks.q: When does 5% weight review trigger?
blocks.a: Compare the current effective actual/profile weight with the saved target basis using absolute percentage difference. Several small changes can accumulate to the threshold; successful refresh resets the basis.
blocks.probe: 80 kg to 76.1 kg versus 76.0 kg?

blocks.q: What is the difference between schema and domain validation?
blocks.a: A schema can require typed fields and arrays. Domain checks enforce exactly the saved slots, realistic internal macro energy, recipe completeness and fixed daily tolerances. Valid JSON alone is insufficient.
blocks.probe: Give an output that passes schema but fails domain checks.

blocks.q: Why do two snacks need distinct IDs?
blocks.a: Their category is the same but their scheduled positions differ. A swap must replace only the selected slot, and completion refers to a specific generated meal instance.
blocks.probe: Explain type, slotId and id.

blocks.q: Is a nutritionProfileKey a security signature?
blocks.a: No. It is deterministic JSON used to compare relevant inputs and detect changes. Authorization comes from token verification and server ownership, not from trusting this string.
blocks.probe: What would a cryptographic signature add, and where would it be verified?

blocks.q: Why keep completed food on rebuild?
blocks.a: A new plan is a suggestion; consumed food is a historical fact. Retaining IDs and calories avoids losing or double-counting the user's actual log.
blocks.probe: What happens to unlogged old meals?

blocks.q: Can the app guarantee allergy safety?
blocks.a: No. It includes allergy constraints in prompts and checks output structure/arithmetic, but does not deterministically verify every ingredient against an allergen database.
blocks.probe: What additional data/validation would you need?

pages.title: AI integration and provider failures
pages.goal: Close each answer and explain it in your own words.

blocks.q: Did you train a model?
blocks.a: No. The app orchestrates an external Gemini model using prompts, structured output, profile context and server validation. It does not train weights or fine-tune a model.
blocks.probe: What is the engineering beyond calling an API?

blocks.q: Is this RAG?
blocks.a: Not in its current form: it has no embedding pipeline or vector retrieval. Saved structured profile/plan context is included directly in requests.
blocks.probe: When might retrieval become useful?

blocks.q: How many model calls does a chat use?
blocks.a: A pure greeting uses zero. An off-topic or whole-plan non-greeting uses one scope call. A relevant follow-up normally uses scope plus answer, two calls. Failures may stop earlier.
blocks.probe: Does an off-topic message cost nothing?

blocks.q: Why exclude assistant messages from classification?
blocks.a: Old assistant instructions or a saved fitness goal should not turn an unrelated latest request into an in-scope task. Recent user messages are only context for follow-ups.
blocks.probe: What if a previous assistant reply was very strict?

blocks.q: Do JSON schemas eliminate hallucinations?
blocks.a: No. They constrain structure, not truth. The backend still checks domain constraints, and ingredient nutrition/allergen suitability remains model-estimated.
blocks.probe: Which facts cannot arithmetic validate?

blocks.q: What happens on a 429?
blocks.a: The adapter maps it to AI_RATE_LIMIT and does not perform an SDK network replay. Nutrition exposes the error; workout/chat retain their older fallback behavior, a known inconsistency.
blocks.probe: Why might retrying immediately worsen the problem?

blocks.q: Why allow one correction of invalid output?
blocks.a: A completed response may be structurally or arithmetically invalid. One bounded correction includes the specific validation error and fixed targets. It is different from replaying a failed transport request.
blocks.probe: What is the maximum for an already-valid-target menu stage?

blocks.q: Does store:false mean no data is ever retained?
blocks.a: It is the Interactions request setting used by this code, not a statement about every provider logging, abuse-monitoring or contractual retention policy. Avoid stronger privacy claims without checking those policies.
blocks.probe: Where is conversation history actually managed?

pages.title: Scale, reliability and judgment
pages.goal: Close each answer and explain it in your own words.

blocks.q: How would you handle many users?
blocks.a: First measure request mix and provider limits. Add per-user budgets/rate limiting, durable idempotency, shared job coordination and indexed/paginated persistence; then scale API workers. Worker-local Maps alone do not coordinate replicas.
blocks.probe: What breaks when a second worker starts?

blocks.q: Can startup retries duplicate a paid plan request?
blocks.a: The startup utility only wraps profile and readiness reads. It does not wrap plan/chat POSTs, and Gemini SDK retries are disabled. A future retry policy needs durable idempotency for write/cost side effects.
blocks.probe: What if the model succeeded but the response was lost?

blocks.q: Can a late response affect the wrong account?
blocks.a: The client aborts on session changes and compares request revisions/UIDs before setting state. Server requests independently verify identity. Cancellation does not undo an already committed write.
blocks.probe: Show the exact revision comparison.

blocks.q: Why is server history not cross-device sync yet?
blocks.a: Database snapshots exist, but Dashboard does not hydrate/merge working logs, swaps and chat from them. A sync design needs stable event IDs, ownership, versions and conflict semantics.
blocks.probe: What wins if two devices edit the same day?

blocks.q: What would you fix first?
blocks.a: Harden workout output ownership/date validation, then make history persistence honest and reliable, then add durable generation idempotency and cost controls. These reduce correctness/security risk before adding extra AI features.
blocks.probe: Which test would prove the first fix?

blocks.q: How would you evaluate chat scope?
blocks.a: Create a labeled set of greetings, relevant follow-ups, unrelated/code requests, whole-plan requests, mixed and adversarial turns. Measure classification errors and cost/latency rather than relying on a few demos.
blocks.probe: Which false positives are most costly?

blocks.q: What is your biggest remaining design tradeoff?
blocks.a: The hybrid persistence model keeps the browser experience simple but limits continuity and recovery. The guide treats it as an explicit limitation, not complete cross-device account history.
blocks.probe: Why not promise full offline support?

blocks.q: How do you prove ownership of AI-assisted code?
blocks.a: Explain an unfamiliar request path, name its invariants and failure cases, make a small change, and add a meaningful test. Be explicit that AI assisted implementation and avoid claiming unearned authorship or impact metrics.
blocks.probe: Can you do that exercise without using AI?

blocks.title: Score each area from 0 to 3
items: Accuracy: distinguishes current implementation from intended behavior.
Traceability: can locate the source and explain the data entering/leaving.
Reasoning: compares alternatives and identifies failure modes.
Practical skill: can write/debug a small change and justify its test.
Integrity: states AI assistance, unknowns and limits without bluffing.

blocks.title: After the practice
blocks.body: Replay unclear answers. For each one, write: claim -> source -> invariant -> counterexample -> test. If your answer depends on memorized wording, practise the same idea with a different example.

pages.title: Your demo and CV checklist
pages.goal: Make the demonstration credible and easy to follow.

blocks.title: A two-minute demo order
items: Show profile preferences and the personal schedule, then the corresponding nutrition screen.
Explain saved targets versus planned totals; show one useful recipe or meal substitution.
Show Training and mark an exercise completed; make clear calorie burn is estimated.
Show Progress with actual/reused/skipped semantics and historical view-only days.
Ask the coach one practical follow-up and one unrelated request to demonstrate scope.
Point out the public walkthrough and explain the cold-start loader if it appears.

blocks.title: Before an interview
blocks.body: Use clearly labeled sample data or your own account; never expose real credentials or another person's health records. Rehearse both warm and unavailable-backend behavior. Know that clearing browser storage removes working history. Do not rely on a live model succeeding at exactly the right moment; have truthful screenshots and explain their sample-data provenance.

blocks.title: CV bullet templates
blocks.body: 1. "Developed an AI-assisted fitness companion with React, Express, MongoDB, Firebase Authentication and Gemini." 2. "Implemented fixed-target nutrition validation, personalized meal-slot contracts and history-preserving plan rebuilding." 3. "Added scoped trainer follow-ups, optional weight journaling and bounded startup read retries." Use implemented/reviewed wording only to the extent it accurately describes your own work and current understanding.

blocks.title: Claims to avoid
blocks.body: Do not claim a self-trained LLM, RAG, body-image analysis, clinical accuracy, guaranteed abuse prevention, automatic cross-device activity sync, production load capacity, or personal authorship of every line. A smaller precise claim is easier to defend.

pages.title: Last-minute revision: twelve invariants
pages.goal: These should survive even if you forget a filename.

blocks.title: Say these without notes
items: Identity comes from a verified server token, not a browser-supplied UID; harden the workout spread exception.
Firebase stores identity; MongoDB stores application records.
Working activity, swaps and chat are still browser-local.
A 500 or timeout is not a missing-profile 404.
Startup retries safe reads, not writes or paid generation calls.
Targets can be reused across days; menus are a separate task.
Custom macros are authoritative; weight review applies to auto targets.
A type can repeat; a slotId must be unique; a meal id tracks an instance.
Valid JSON is not valid nutrition, and arithmetic is not clinical truth.
Pure greeting: 0 model calls; redirect: 1; relevant follow-up: normally 2.
Measured, reused and skipped are different states; scale change is not fat loss.
A Promise Map is worker-local coordination, not durable global idempotency.

blocks.title: Answer structure for almost any question
blocks.body: Start with what this code does. Point to a source location. Explain the tradeoff. Give a failure case and a test. If you do not know, say what you would inspect rather than inventing an answer.

pages.title: Glossary: browser and API language
pages.goal: Translate vocabulary into project behavior.

blocks.title: Terms used in this guide
rows: A browser app whose route changes render React views; Vercel must serve index.html for deep links.
A React function that renders UI from props/state, such as DietCard.
Inputs/callbacks passed into a component; they are not a persistence mechanism.
Values that drive a component render, such as the selected training date.
A computed value, such as burn from completed IDs, rather than a second independently edited copy.
A function captures values from a render; setters do not change those captured values immediately.
Unsubscribe/abort/invalidate when the effect or component is replaced.
Shared React session data; separate from the database.
Machine-readable request outcome; 401, 404, 409, 429 and 503 mean different things.
A credential carried in Authorization; verify it before trusting its UID.
Signed token format; reading a payload is not signature verification.
Browser cross-origin access policy, not a substitute for authentication.
Express function that can verify a request and call next before the controller.
HTTP input/output and orchestration boundary, such as saveCheckIn.
Provider client library; geminiClient wraps the official Google SDK.

pages.title: Glossary: data and AI language
pages.goal: Use the right word for the guarantee you actually have.

blocks.title: Terms used in this guide
rows: A structural definition for a database document or model response.
Business rules beyond field types, such as exact slots and daily macro bounds.
Transforming acceptable input/output into a consistent representation.
Update a matching record or insert it if absent.
Enforces uniqueness of a combination, such as userId plus date.
Stored state of a generated plan at a point in time.
Loading persisted data into client working state; server plan hydration is not implemented.
Repeating an operation does not create extra intended effects; not provided globally for generation.
Sharing one in-flight Promise for matching concurrent work in a worker.
A write succeeds only if selected stored values still match an expected state.
A database unit of work committed or rolled back as a group; Promise.all is not one.
Untrusted text tries to redirect model behavior; prompt instructions alone cannot guarantee prevention.
A request for schema-shaped model output; domain checks still run afterward.
Retrieval-augmented generation; no embedding/vector retrieval system exists here.
The service is starting after inactivity; handled through visible UI and bounded safe reads.
